questions.q: Why are embeddings described as unusually cacheable?
options: They are cheap to compute but change constantly, so caches need aggressive TTLs
They are expensive to compute yet perfectly deterministic — the same text through the same model always yields the same vector
They compress well with gzip, so storage costs are negligible
They expire predictably after 24 hours, making invalidation trivial
questions.explain: Embedding inference is expensive (API money plus 100–300ms, or GPU time) and deterministic — the textbook definition of cacheable, and the cache never goes stale on its own unless the model changes.

questions.q: What cache invalidation policy does the chapter prescribe for embedding vectors?
options: Refresh the cache nightly regardless of model changes
Invalidate on every query to guarantee correctness
Set a 1-hour TTL on all cached embeddings to keep them fresh
Never set a TTL — vectors do not decay; namespace keys by model ID and treat invalidation as a model-versioning problem
questions.explain: Embedding vectors never go stale on their own, so expiry would only cause pointless recomputation; invalidation is handled by model ID namespacing, not TTLs.

questions.q: What happens if a query path reads a cached vector whose model ID does not match the consuming model?
options: Retrieval quality degrades silently with no error — cross-model vector reads are silent corruption
SQL Server raises a dimension-mismatch error immediately
The cache automatically re-embeds the text with the correct model
The query falls back to full-text search
questions.explain: Cross-model vector reads are silent corruption: the query runs, numbers look plausible, and retrieval quality degrades without an error — which is why every cache key must include the model ID.

questions.q: Which three cache layers does the chapter recommend, in order from fastest to most durable?
options: DNS cache, TCP cache, and page cache
CDN cache, browser cache, and blob storage
In-process LRU cache, Redis (shared), and a SQL Server persistent cache with native VECTOR
GPU cache, NVMe cache, and tape backup
questions.explain: The architecture layers caches: in-process LRU for the hottest questions, Redis for cross-instance sharing with sub-millisecond latency, and SQL Server native VECTOR for durability, auditability, and joins against relational data.

questions.q: For a semantic answer cache in SQL Server, what similarity threshold should you start at, and how should it be tuned?
options: Start at 0.08 cosine distance and measure the false-hit rate on your eval set, widening it only with evidence
Start at 0.90 cosine distance and tighten it until cache hits drop
Use Euclidean distance 1.0 as a fixed universal threshold
Thresholds are unnecessary because semantic caches never produce false hits
questions.explain: The chapter says the threshold is everything: start at 0.08 cosine distance, measure the false-hit rate on the eval set, and only widen it with evidence — too loose returns wrong answers to paraphrased questions.
